schools.summary: Ellicott: the verse is identical with 2 Kings 16:2, but the LXX/Syriac/Arabic read 'twenty-five,' easing the chronology with Hezekiah's age (2 Chron 29:1); the Assyrian monuments call Ahaz Yahuhazi (Jehoahaz).
Gill notes Ahaz was twenty at his accession, the verse standing as in the parallel at 2 Kings 16:2.
Clarke lays out the whole arc of the sixteen-year reign of apostasy in a breath, referring the chronology to 2 Kings 16:2.
Henry frames the chapter as the wicked reign of Ahaz: sinners left to their lusts grow more desperate, and the progress of wickedness is rapid.

debates.question: Was Ahaz twenty or twenty-five years old at his accession?

sides.position: twenty-five (LXX, Syriac, Arabic), easing the chronology with Hezekiah's age

schools.summary: Keil reads 'walked in the ways of the kings of Israel' as the master-charge and 'molten images for the Baalim' as manufactured idols outrunning the calves; Ellicott renders 'for the Baals' (the god's several avatars), calls the clause the chronicler's own addition explaining the state Baal-worship imported through Ahab's house, possibly fallen out of Kings.

themes: the ways of the kings of Israel

schools.summary: Ellicott names Moloch and the valley of Hinnom (Solomon's high place, 1 Kings 11:5; Jer. 7:31), traces 'Ge-hinnom' to the Gehenna of the NT, and reads 'burned his children' as the chronicler's paraphrase (a letter-transposition) with a generalizing plural, against Thenius's charge of exaggeration.
Clarke preserves the Targum's legend that the Word of the Lord snatched Hezekiah from the fire of Tophet, stringing together the great deliverances from fire from Abram to the three in Babylon.

outliers.note: Reports at length the Targum's midrash that Hezekiah escaped the flames into which Ahaz cast his children, because the three confessors were to proceed from him.

schools.summary: Ellicott shows the chronicler subordinates history to the didactic aim, selecting two open-field defeats to display God's chastisement; Rezin of Damascus 'smote in' Ahaz's army (cf. Isa. 7:2), and even Thenius owned the section thoroughly historical.
Wesley: God was Ahaz's God by sovereign dominion, not special relation, which Ahaz had renounced; Clarke refers to the joint campaign of Rezin and Pekah at 2 Kings 16:5.
Gill reads 'the LORD his God' as God's by right, by the national covenant, and by Ahaz's own hypocritical profession — a rebuke, not a compliment.

Keil grounds the slaughter in the people's forsaking the LORD and defends the figures against the critics (Gesenius, De Wette, Winer), since the allies aimed at annihilation (Isa. 7:6); Ellicott reads 'in one day' as one engagement, a third of the host of 2 Chron 26:13.
Clarke doubts 120,000 could fall in one day though all copies agree; Wesley draws the poetic justice — God made the kings of Israel, whom Ahaz imitated, the scourge of Judah.
Gill names Pekah son of Remaliah as the agent and lets the figure stand.

debates.question: Is the number of 120,000 slain historically reliable?

sides.position: reliable — the war aimed at Judah's annihilation, and the Ephraimites were extremely cruel
scarcely credible for a single day, though all versions agree
an exaggeration of the wonder-loving chronicler
holders: Gesenius, De Wette, Winer (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

themes: a hundred and twenty thousand slain
because they had forsaken the LORD

schools.summary: Keil takes Maaseiah 'the king's son' as a royal kinsman (Ahaz too young to have an adult son), Azrikam as governor of the palace, and Elkanah as grand vizier; Ellicott adds that the three are named because the blow that struck them struck the king whose punishment is being told.
Gill notes Maaseiah must have escaped the fire of the valley of Hinnom, now falling instead to Zichri's sword.

themes: the death of the king's son

schools.summary: Keil stresses the emphatic 'their brethren' and defends the figures against the critics (Gesenius, De Wette, Winer) by the annihilating design of Isa. 7:6; Ellicott corroborates the 200,000 by Sennacherib's boast of 200,150 captives, and notes Kings omits both deportations.
Gill explains the vast captivity followed easily once the fighting men had been slaughtered.

debates.question: Are the round numbers of captives an exaggeration?

sides.position: reliable — matched by the war's temper and by Sennacherib's parallel boast of 200,150 captives

holders: Gesenius, De Wette, Winer (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

schools.summary: Keil presents Oded as a prophet of the true God (like Hosea) who met the host as Azariah met Asa (2 Chron 15:2); Ellicott sharpens his argument — the victory was God's punitive wrath, not their valour, and their rage 'reaches to heaven' like Abel's blood (Gen. 4:10).
Wesley reads the 'rage' as crying to God for vengeance; Clarke praises the speech as simple, humane, and convincing, proof of the humanity still in the chiefs of Ephraim.
Henry: Israel conquered only as the rod of God's indignation against Judah — it ill becomes sinners to be cruel, nor could they hope for mercy while showing none.
Gill distinguishes this Oded from the earlier prophet of Asa's day.

themes: victory as God's wrath, not valour

schools.summary: Keil weighs the emphatic 'sons of Judah' and the doubled 'you, even you' — are there not sins with you against the LORD? Ellicott renders the abrupt question 'are you the only guiltless people?', pointing to Israel's own calves of Bethel and Dan.
Henry turns the verse into a principle: slavery is against the law of love and the gospel of grace; none can hold a brother in bondage without breaking the golden rule (Matt. 7:12).
Gill: the purpose to keep brethren as bondmen and bondwomen was flatly contrary to the law.

themes: slavery against the law of love

schools.summary: Keil: the carrying-away of the women and children filled up the measure of Israel's guilt, so the fierce wrath of Jahve hung over them unless they sent the captives back; Ellicott notes the illative 'and now' and that Lev. 25:39 forbids the permanent enslaving of Israelites.
Gill hears in 'hear me' a call not merely to attend but to obey.
Henry marks the outcome: God commands them to release the prisoners, and they obeyed.

themes: the fierce wrath of the LORD

schools.summary: Keil records that four named Ephraimite chiefs, moved by Oded's speech, placed themselves at the head of the people to meet the returning army; Ellicott explains 'children of Ephraim' as the prophets' name for the ten tribes and 'stood up against' as confronting, an interposition to bar the captives.
Gill notes the principal men of the ten tribes now come forward, their names following.

Keil renders the plea — add not to our sins, for a great trespass and fierce wrath already lie upon Israel; Ellicott weighs the disputed opening clause but finds the elders openly admitting an existing trespass they will not aggravate.
Gill fixes 'hither' as into Samaria, near which the army stood.
Ellicott identifies the parties: the armed men are the host, the princes the four named heads, and 'the congregation' the citizens assembled at the gate of Samaria.
Gill records that the soldiers left both captives and spoil for the princes to dispose of, such was the effect of the prophet's word.
Wesley: to leave the captives showed a more truly heroic bravery than to take them — it is true honour to yield to reason and religion against one's interest.

themes: an army yielding to a word

schools.summary: Keil paints the compassion — clothing, food, anointing, the feeble set on asses to Jericho; Ellicott reads the echoes (the anointing as at Luke 7:38), a rebuke to the later Samaritans (Neh. 4:2), the anticipation of the good Samaritan (Luke 10:30), and the parallel of Oded with Shemaiah (1 Kings 12:22).
Gill takes the men 'expressed by name' as the chiefs or others appointed to the work.
Wesley: those 'expressed by name' were appointed to manage the business.

themes: works of mercy to the captives
an enemy treated as a brother

schools.summary: Ellicott reads 'kings of Assyria' as a generalized plural, all versions having 'king'; Keil grants it rhetorical (like 'Baalim') but finds in it the tragedy — Ahaz spurned the LORD's help offered at Isa. 7:4 and turned to the world-power, from whom no real help could come.
Clarke notes the versions and the parallel (2 Kings 16:7) read 'king,' meaning Tiglath-pileser; Wesley takes the 'kings' as princes so styled.
Gill refers 'kings' to Tiglath-pileser and his son, noting the versions read the singular.

debates.question: Is 'kings of Assyria' a copyist's plural or a rhetorical one?

sides.position: a plural to be corrected to the singular of the versions and the parallel (one king, Tiglath-pileser)
a rhetorical plural, like 'Baalim,' expressing Ahaz's turn to the world-power

schools.summary: Keil renders 'and besides' — the Edomites, held in vassalage by Amaziah and Uzziah (2 Chron 25:11; 26:2) but freed by Rezin (2 Kings 16:6), seized the moment to defeat Judah and take revenge; Ellicott traces the same sequence to the loss of Elath and the emboldening disasters of Ahaz.
Gill notes the Edomites came again, as in Jehoshaphat's day, and carried off captives.

Keil: the Philistines whom Uzziah had subdued (2 Chron 26:6) used the pressure on Judah to plunder and enlarge their borders, taking Bethshemesh, Ajalon, Gederoth, Shocho (2 Chron 11:7), Timnah, and Gimzo; Ellicott fixes the shephelah and Negeb and reads 'they dwelt there' as permanent occupation.
Gill sets the invasion in the Philistines' revenge for Uzziah's earlier conquests.

themes: cities of the lowland and the south

schools.summary: Keil calls 'king of Israel' bitter irony on the name of God's people; Ellicott sees irony plus the chronicler's usage where Judah is the true 'Israel' (2 Chron 21:2), and renders 'made Judah naked' as 'dealt licentiously' with 'transgressed sore' = did unfaithfulness.
Wesley: they that will not humble themselves under God's word are humbled by his judgments; 'naked' = stripped of treasure, strongholds, religion, and divine protection.
Gill reads 'king of Israel' of Ahaz's northern ways and rule over Israel's tribes (some versions 'Judah'); 'made naked' = stripped of religion and protection.
Henry: the LORD brought Judah low, for those who will not humble themselves under God's word are justly humbled by his judgments.

debates.question: Why is Ahaz called 'king of Israel'?

sides.position: bitter irony on the name of the people of God
the chronicler's pregnant usage in which Judah is the true 'Israel'
literal — he walked in the ways of Israel's kings and ruled Israel's tribes (some versions read 'Judah')

themes: the enemies as rods in God's hand

schools.summary: Ellicott recounts from the monuments how Tiglath-pileser took Damascus and slew Rezin (2 Kings 16:9-10) but only to extend his empire, reducing Judah to a tributary dependency (2 Kings 18:7); Keil keeps the pointed antithesis — he distressed him but strengthened him not.
Gill sets the meeting at Damascus, which the Assyrian took, rather than at Jerusalem.
Wesley: by removing the Syrian bulwark the Assyrian only smoothed his own road toward Judah, a far more dangerous enemy, as the next reign proved.

themes: a protector who became a master

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'Ahaz had despoiled' the house of the LORD, the king, and the princes (the great courtiers) for the tribute (2 Kings 16:8), and reads 'helped him not' as bringing no advantage but hastening ruin — the Assyrians' principle being plunder (cf. 2 Kings 16:17).
Gill itemizes the bribe drawn from the temple treasures, the royal treasury, and a levy on the princes.
Clarke: the Assyrian did Ahaz no ultimate service (cf. 2 Kings 16:9).
Henry: wicked men have no real affection for those who revolt to them, nor care to do them a kindness.

themes: the temple stripped for a bribe

schools.summary: Ellicott fixes the moment at Ahaz's homage-visit to Damascus (2 Kings 16:10) and hears in 'he, king Ahaz' a deliberate, emphatic naming of the notorious apostate for lasting infamy.
Gill: in his distress Ahaz trespassed yet more, increasing his idolatries in imitation of what he saw at Damascus.
Wesley pours out indignation: 'that Ahaz,' a monster and reproach of mankind, whom even grievous afflictions made worse, whose name deserves to be detested for ever.
Henry: 'that wretched man' — those are wicked indeed who are made worse by their afflictions, trespassing yet more in their distress.

themes: affliction has no saving virtue in itself

schools.summary: Keil corrects the tense — the participle is present ('who smite him'), Ahaz sacrificing during the war, not after; Ellicott asks whether the chronicler thought the gods real, cites the common belief and Paul's 'sacrifice to demons' (1 Cor. 10:20; Deut. 32:17), and notes the gods 'were the ruin of him.'
Gill refuses to let the Spirit ascribe the defeat to idols: the sense is the gods of the men of Damascus who smote him.
Clarke, following Hallet, adopts the older Hebrew/Greek reading that makes 'which have smitten me' Ahaz's own deluded words, not the historian's judgment.
Henry: no marvel men's devotions are misplaced when they mistake the author of their trouble and of their help.

debates.question: How is 'the gods of Damascus which smote him' to be read?

sides.position: repoint/emend so the mad assertion is Ahaz's own words, not the historian's — for God would not ascribe defeat to idols
keep the text — a present participle describing the Syrians defeating Ahaz, reflecting the age's belief in the gods' reality (demons)

themes: the props that became the ruin

schools.summary: Keil describes the deliberate sacrilege — mutilating the court furniture, cutting the panels and taking down the brazen sea (2 Kings 16:17), then shutting the doors to suppress the service; Ellicott reads 'cut in pieces' as 'trimmed' off the metal and the closed doors as those of the sanctuary itself.
Gill reads the mercenary motive: Ahaz melted or sold the vessels for money, his own treasures exhausted.
Clarke: the worship stood totally suspended, the doors shut, until Hezekiah reopened them (2 Chron 29:3).

themes: the seam of hope in Hezekiah

schools.summary: Keil keeps to the verse's verdict — high places in every city provoking the covenant God to anger; Ellicott anchors 'provoked to anger' in Deut. 32:16 and ties the multiplied shrines to the temple-changes Ahaz made to satisfy the Assyrian.
Gill sees a calculated policy: the country high places were meant to keep the people from resorting to the shut temple at Jerusalem.
Henry: the progress of wickedness is rapid, and it is an awful thing to reflect upon a sinner driven away in his wickedness into the eternal world.

Ellicott notes the chronicler has varied his usual closing formula ('all his ways, first and last'; cf. 2 Chron 25:26; 26:7; 2 Kings 16:19) and names the source, the book of the kings of Judah and Israel; Keil takes the verse as the formal head of the reign's ending.
Gill treats the notice as matter already handled, deferring the details to the parallel record.

themes: the book of the kings of Judah and Israel

schools.summary: Keil reads the phrasing 'in the city, in Jerusalem' (not 'with David') as a deliberate slight — Ahaz denied the royal tombs because he had not walked like David; Ellicott marks the clause as peculiar to the chronicler (cf. 2 Chron 21:20) and rejects Thenius's guess of a mistake or later legalism for a genuine written source.
Clarke: the writer commonly puts 'Israel' for Judah, regarding the two as one people of one stock.
